title: Electricity + Magnets = Spin
description: Everything ARIA does to move comes down to one trick from physics, wired to a chassis.

content.value: Run current through a wire and it creates a small magnetic field around itself — that's not a robotics fact, it's a plain physics fact, true of any wire, anywhere. Put that wire near a fixed magnet, arranged the right way, and the two magnetic fields push and pull against each other. Shape the wire into a loop that's free to turn, and that push becomes rotation.

current through a coil  -->  coil becomes a magnet
coil's magnet vs the fixed magnet's poles  -->  push/pull
mounted so it can spin  -->  the push becomes rotation

That's the entire idea behind a DC motor. Everything in the next lesson — brushes, a commutator, coils — exists purely to keep that push happening continuously as the coil spins past the point where it would otherwise stop and settle.
Why This Matters for a Robot

Motors are how a robot turns a THINK decision into an ACT in the physical world. Everything else in this module — driver chips, wheels, differential steering — is really just plumbing around this one spinning trick, getting it wired safely and steered usefully.

Reverse the current direction and the push reverses too — that single fact is why swapping two wires on a motor makes it spin the opposite way. You'll use exactly this in the H-bridge lesson coming up.

Key takeaway: current through a coil creates a magnetic field; placed near a fixed magnet, that field pushes, and mounted to spin, the push becomes rotation. That's the entire physics behind every motor on ARIA.

quiz.question: What creates the magnetic field inside a motor's spinning coil?
options: Current flowing through the coil's wire
The coil being made of metal
quiz.explain: Any current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field around itself — that's the whole starting point of a motor.

quiz.question: What happens if you reverse the direction of current through a motor?
quiz.explain: Reversing current reverses the coil's magnetic field, which flips which way it's pushed relative to the fixed magnet.
